questions.stem: A client's last menstrual period began on May 1, 2026. Using Naegele's rule, what is the estimated date of birth?

rationale.correct: Naegele's rule: first day of the LMP + 7 days − 3 months + 1 year.

perOption.a: Add 7 days (May 8), subtract 3 months (February 8) and add 1 year.
perOption.c: This adds 3 months instead of subtracting.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.educationalObjective: Calculate an estimated date of birth.

questions.stem: Which finding is a positive (certain) sign of pregnancy?

options.text: Fetal heart tones heard with a Doppler
Hegar's sign (softening of the lower uterus)

rationale.correct: Positive signs: fetal heart tones, fetal movement felt by the examiner and fetus seen on ultrasound.

perOption.a: Only signs coming directly from the fetus are positive signs.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)

questions.stem: A pregnant client has a 4-year-old born at 39 weeks, had a miscarriage at 10 weeks, and has 2-year-old twins born at 34 weeks. Which GTPAL is correct?

rationale.correct: GTPAL: Gravida, Term, Preterm, Abortions, Living. Multiples count once for G, T and P.

perOption.a: 4 pregnancies (including this one), 1 term birth, 1 preterm birth (twins count as one), 1 abortion and 3 living children.
perOption.b: Twins count as one preterm birth.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)

questions.stem: A client is planning a pregnancy. Which supplement should the nurse recommend?

options.text: Folic acid 400 mcg daily, starting before conception

rationale.correct: Folic acid at least 1 month before conception and through early pregnancy prevents neural tube defects.

perOption.a: Folic acid reduces the risk of neural tube defects.

questions.stem: A pregnant client wakes at night with leg cramps. What should the nurse suggest?

options.text: Straighten the leg and pull the toes up toward the knee (dorsiflex the foot)

rationale.correct: Leg cramps: dorsiflexion, stretching, hydration and adequate calcium and magnesium.

perOption.a: Dorsiflexion stretches the calf muscle and relieves the cramp.
perOption.c: Vigorous massage isn't advised if DVT is possible.

questions.stem: A client at 32 weeks lying flat on her back becomes dizzy, pale and sweaty. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Turn her onto her left side

rationale.correct: Supine hypotensive syndrome: lateral (left) positioning.

perOption.a: This relieves pressure of the uterus on the vena cava (supine hypotension).

questions.stem: Which danger signs should a pregnant client report right away? Select all that apply.

options.text: A gush or leak of fluid from the vagina
Mild ankle swelling at the end of the day

rationale.correct: Teach danger signs: bleeding, fluid leakage, headache or vision changes, decreased movement, fever and severe abdominal pain.

perOption.a: These may signal preeclampsia.
perOption.b: Bleeding may signal previa, abruption or miscarriage.
perOption.c: This may be rupture of membranes.

questions.stem: When is a pregnant client without risk factors routinely screened for gestational diabetes?

rationale.correct: GDM screening at 24 to 28 weeks (earlier if high risk).

perOption.a: Insulin resistance rises in the second trimester.
perOption.b: This is early screening, for high-risk clients only.

questions.stem: A client with gestational diabetes asks about effects on her baby. Which risk should the nurse explain?

options.text: A large baby and low blood sugar after birth
Low birth weight from too little insulin

rationale.correct: GDM: macrosomia, birth injury, newborn hypoglycemia; good glucose control reduces the risks.

perOption.a: Maternal hyperglycemia causes fetal hyperinsulinemia, macrosomia and newborn hypoglycemia.

questions.stem: A client at 34 weeks has a blood pressure of 164/112 mm Hg, a severe headache and spots before her eyes. What does the nurse suspect?

rationale.correct: Severe features: BP 160/110 or higher, headache, vision changes, RUQ pain, low platelets, raised liver enzymes, pulmonary edema, rising creatinine.

perOption.a: Severe-range blood pressure with neurologic symptoms indicates severe features.
perOption.b: New symptoms after 20 weeks suggest preeclampsia.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)

questions.stem: A client receiving IV magnesium sulfate for preeclampsia has a respiratory rate of 10/min and absent knee reflexes. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Document the findings and reassess in 1 hour

rationale.correct: Magnesium: monitor RR (12 or more), reflexes, urine output (30 mL/hr or more) and level of consciousness. The antidote is calcium gluconate.

perOption.a: These signs show magnesium toxicity; stopping the infusion comes first, then calcium gluconate and the provider.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client with preeclampsia has right upper quadrant pain, a platelet count of 85,000/mm3 and high liver enzymes. Which complication does the nurse suspect?

rationale.correct: HELLP is a severe variant of preeclampsia; delivery is often needed.

perOption.a: Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes and Low Platelets.
perOption.b: This doesn't explain the low platelets.

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is more consistent with placenta previa or placental abruption.

rows.text: Recent car crash or cocaine use
Bleeding may be hidden behind the placenta

rationale.correct: Previa: painless, bright red, no vaginal exams. Abruption: painful, rigid uterus, possibly concealed bleeding.

perOption.r1:c1: Previa typically causes painless bright red bleeding.
perOption.r2:c1: The uterus is soft in previa.
perOption.r2:c2: Bleeding behind the placenta causes a rigid, tender uterus.
perOption.r3:c2: Trauma and cocaine are risk factors for abruption.
perOption.r4:c2: Concealed bleeding can occur with abruption.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)

questions.stem: A client at 30 weeks has painless, bright red vaginal bleeding. Which action should the nurse avoid?

rationale.correct: Suspected previa: no vaginal exams until the placenta location is known by ultrasound.

perOption.a: A vaginal exam can cause hemorrhage with placenta previa.

questions.stem: A client at 7 weeks gestation has sharp pain on one side of the lower abdomen, light vaginal spotting and new right shoulder pain. What does the nurse suspect?

rationale.correct: A ruptured ectopic pregnancy is an emergency (hemorrhage); prepare for surgery.

perOption.a: Shoulder pain suggests blood in the abdomen irritating the diaphragm.
perOption.c: This doesn't explain the shoulder pain.
perOption.d: This occurs later in pregnancy without shoulder pain.

questions.stem: A client at 10 weeks gestation has vomited many times a day for a week, has lost 6% of her body weight and has ketones in her urine. What should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Telling her this is normal morning sickness

perOption.a: Hyperemesis gravidarum causes dehydration and needs rehydration.

questions.stem: An Rh-negative client at 28 weeks has a negative antibody screen (indirect Coombs). What should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Giving it to the baby instead

rationale.correct: Rho(D) immune globulin: at 28 weeks, within 72 hours after birth of an Rh-positive infant, and after any bleeding or invasive procedure.

perOption.a: Rho(D) immune globulin at 28 weeks prevents sensitization.
perOption.d: It is given to the mother.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)

rationale.correct: NST at 32 weeks or more: reactive = 2 or more accelerations of 15 beats for 15 seconds within 20 minutes.

perOption.a: Two or more accelerations of 15 beats for 15 seconds in 20 minutes is reactive.
